t: The first session of the United Nations General Assembly convened at the Methodist Central Hall in London with representatives from 51 member states.
The first session of the United Nations General Assembly convened in London with representatives from the original 51 member states.
The People's Republic of Albania was proclaimed, with Enver Hoxha as the country's de facto head of state.
President Harry S. Truman signed the Rescission Act, annulling benefits payable to Filipino troops who fought for the U.S. during World War II.
Thirty-three people were killed in a human crush at Burnden Park, a football stadium in Bolton, England.
The Los Angeles Rams signed Kenny Washington, making him the first African-American player in the National Football League since 1933.
The US Department of State released the Acheson–Lilienthal Report, a proposal for the international control of nuclear weapons.
Nakam, a Jewish organization seeking revenge for the Holocaust, attempted to poison thousands of SS prisoners at Langwasser internment camp, but did not kill anyone.
The final session of the League of Nations concluded in Geneva, with delegates agreeing to transfer much of its assets to the United Nations.
Two passenger trains collided in Naperville, Illinois, leaving 45 people dead and some 125 injured.
Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita founded the telecommunications corporation Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, later renamed Sony.

While working with a mass of plutonium known as the demon core, Manhattan Project physicist Louis Slotin accidentally exposed himself to a lethal dose of hard radiation, making him the second victim of a criticality accident in history.
Canada's largest recorded onshore earthquake struck Vancouver Island, British Columbia.
Named after Bikini Atoll, the site of the nuclear-weapons test Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, the modern bikini was introduced at a fashion show in Paris.
After weeks of unrest, rioters lynched Bolivian president Gualberto Villarroel, desecrating and hanging his corpse in the streets of La Paz.
Several days of anti-Jewish rioting began in Bratislava, instigated by former Slovak partisans opposed to the restitution of Jewish property after the Holocaust in Slovakia.

The Soviet Union informed Turkey that the way in which the latter was handling the Turkish Straits no longer represented the security interests of Turkey's fellow Black Sea nations, escalating the Turkish Straits crisis.
Widespread riots between Hindus and Muslims took place in Calcutta following the All-India Muslim League's call for an independent Pakistan.
The interim government of India, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, was formed to assist the transition of India from British rule to independence.
Mensa, the largest and oldest high-IQ society in the world, was formed in the United Kingdom.
Il Canto degli Italiani is adopted as national anthem by the newly formed Italian Republic.
Inter-religious riots in which Hindu mobs targeted Muslim families began in the Indian state of Bihar, resulting in thousands of deaths.
U.S.-backed Iranian troops brought an end to the Iran crisis when they marched on the breakaway Republic of Mahabad and recaptured the territory.
American gangster Bugsy Siegel opened The Flamingo Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas, the oldest casino still in operation on the Las Vegas Strip.
